items.title: Pulsar discovery near Milky Way's center could test Einstein's relativity

featured_image.name: Say hello to Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the center of ...

items.description:
A flurry of findings from international research teams is prompting astronomers to reconsider long-held assumptions about the Milky Way's center and the nature of cosmic cataclysms observed by space telescopes.

A study published this week in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society proposes that the object at the heart of our galaxy may not be a supermassive black hole at all, but rather an ultra-dense clump of exotic dark matter. The research challenges the prevailing theory that Sagittarius A* — long believed to be a black hole with roughly 4 million times the mass of the Sun — is responsible for the extreme orbits of nearby stars racing at thousands of kilometers per second.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: Trump considers second carrier if Iran talks fail

featured_image.name: Trump says he might send second carrier for Iran strikes if talks fail

items.description:
The United States and Iran held their first nuclear negotiations since the 12-day war in June 2025, meeting indirectly in Muscat, Oman on February 6 with Omani officials serving as intermediaries. The talks mark a potential thaw after months of heightened tensions, though major disputes over uranium enrichment remain unresolved.

President Donald Trump described the discussions as "very good" and committed to further rounds of talks, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called them "a good start," despite acknowledging that significant work remains to establish trust between the two nations. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei characterized the half-day meeting as "a way to measure the seriousness of the other side" and to determine how the process could continue.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Carney says call with Trump on Gordie Howe Bridge was 'positive'

featured_image.name: Carney says he told Trump Canada paid for Gordie Howe Bridge

items.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with President Donald Trump on Tuesday morning about the Gordie Howe International Bridge after Trump threatened to block its opening, describing the conversation as "positive" and expressing optimism the matter would be resolved.[1][2][3]

The call came after Trump declared on his Truth Social platform Monday evening that he would "not permit" the bridge linking Windsor, Ontario, to Detroit, Michigan, to open until the United States is "fully compensated for everything we have given" Canada. Trump also demanded the U.S. receive ownership of "at least one half of this asset."[4][5][6][1]

items.title: Data center electricity demand to triple by 2035, new study finds

featured_image.name: Aerial top down view of a big data center in Middenmeer, the Netherlands.  stock video 1879460253

items.description:
The world's data centers are poised to consume roughly three times their current electricity by 2035, driven by the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing, according to new industry projections. Renewable energy and nuclear power are expected to supply the majority of this increased demand, even as grid infrastructure struggles to keep pace.

A report from Precedence Research published this week projects that global data center electricity consumption will climb from approximately 460 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2024 to more than 1,300 TWh by 2035. BloombergNEF's December 2025 forecast similarly estimated that U.S. data center power demand alone will reach 106 gigawatts by 2035, up from 40 gigawatts today—a nearly threefold increase.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Police, protesters clash in Sydney as Israeli president’s visit sparks unrest

featured_image.name: Thousands Protest Israeli President Herzog's Visit to Australia

items.description:
Police and protesters clashed violently in central Sydney on Monday evening during demonstrations against Israeli President Isaac Herzog's visit to Australia, with 27 people arrested and at least nine facing criminal charges, including allegations of assaulting officers.[1][2][3]

Approximately 6,000 people gathered at Sydney's Town Hall for what organizers, the Palestine Action Group, described as a peaceful rally opposing Herzog's four-day trip to Australia. As speeches concluded, demonstrators expressed their intention to march toward the NSW Parliament, defying protest restrictions that had been imposed under emergency powers following December's Bondi Beach terror attack.[2][3][4]

items.title: China's Einstein Probe captures first likely black hole-white dwarf collision

featured_image.name: Impossible' pair of vampire stars discovered by Einstein ...

items.description:
China's Einstein Probe space telescope has detected what scientists believe to be the first direct observation of an intermediate-mass black hole tearing apart and consuming a white dwarf star, according to a study published this month in Science Bulletin.[1][2]

The extraordinary cosmic event, designated EP250702a, was detected on July 2, 2025, during a routine sky survey. Scientists discovered that X-ray emissions from the source appeared nearly 24 hours before NASA's Fermi satellite recorded associated gamma-ray bursts—a sequence that immediately distinguished it from ordinary cosmic explosions.[2][1]

items.title: Study finds Earth's core may hold 45 oceans' worth of hydrogen

featured_image.name: Earth's core contains up to 45 times more hydrogen than the ...

items.description:
A new study has found that Earth's core could contain up to 45 times more hydrogen than all the planet's oceans combined, a discovery that reshapes understanding of where our world's water came from. The research, published in Nature Communications, suggests that most of Earth's water has been with the planet since its formation approximately 4.5 billion years ago rather than being delivered later by comets and asteroids.[1][2]

"It really changes the way we think of where our water comes from," said Hilke Schlichting, a professor of Earth, planetary and space science at the University of California, Los Angeles, who was not involved in the study.[1]

items.title: NASA taps Infleqtion to fly first quantum gravity sensor to space

featured_image.name: NASA developing 1st-ever space-based quantum sensor for gravity measurements

items.description:
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has selected quantum technology company Infleqtion to collaborate on a mission that will deploy the world's first quantum gravity sensor in orbit. The Quantum Gravity Gradiometer Pathfinder (QGGPf) mission, backed by more than $20 million in contracted funding, is expected to launch in 2030 for a one-year demonstration in low Earth orbit.[1][2][3]

The announcement, made Monday, marks a major step forward in U.S. leadership in space-based quantum sensing. The satellite mission will test technologies designed to measure subtle variations in Earth's gravitational field, monitoring mass dynamics across the planet's surface including changes in water, ice, and land resources.[4][2][1]

items.title: Astronomers report possible pulsar near Milky Way's black hole

featured_image.name: Probing the spacetime of Sgr A* with pulsar timing

items.description:
Astronomers may have detected a millisecond pulsar in the innermost region of the Milky Way's Galactic Center, a finding that could provide an unprecedented tool for testing Einstein's theory of General Relativity if confirmed. The discovery, announced Monday in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal, represents one of the most sensitive pulsar searches ever conducted toward the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*.[1][2]

A research team led by Karen Perez, a recent Columbia University PhD graduate, used the Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope in West Virginia as part of the Breakthrough Listen initiative to conduct more than 20 hours of observations targeting the galactic center. The survey included 11 hours focused on the innermost 1.4 arcminutes of the region between May 2021 and December 2023.[2][1]

items.title: Russia says peace deal impossible without its own security guarantees

featured_image.name: Senior Russian official says Moscow needs 'security guarantees'

items.description:
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko declared on Tuesday that any peace settlement in Ukraine must include security guarantees for Moscow, describing such assurances as a fundamental condition for ending the nearly four-year conflict.

"We recognise that a peace settlement in Ukraine must take account of Ukraine's security interests, but a key factor, of course, is Russia's security interests," Grushko told the Russian outlet Izvestia on February 10. "If you look carefully and study the statements made by the leaders of the European Union, no one talks about security guarantees for Russia. This is a key element of a peace accord. Without it, an agreement is impossible."[1][2]
